criteria.name: answers_prompt
criteria.reason: Takes a clear position on the single-part prompt: 'the world should make this the central structural adaptation it pursues', then backs it with three named decisions and a rebuttal of the strongest objection.

criteria.name: specificity
criteria.reason: Sources a reader can check: Goldman Sachs '300 million full-time jobs', WEF 2025 '22% ... by 2030', RAND 'sixty-two schools', Harvard 2025 RCT, Horace Mann in 1837. The PLOS ONE claim that '28% of US children aged 6 to 17 never use the internet at home or school' needs checking against the source, and it is about access, not the achievement gap it is meant to prove.

criteria.name: human_voice
criteria.reason: Heavy antithesis: 'not as an average', 'rather than a product', 'enhances rather than divides', 'how things are learned, not what', 'not wholesale replacement... It is directional'. Also a mangled 'not only... rather', em dashes in 'modality—text, visualization, simulation—', 'The shared core remains; the path to it varies.', 'Moving too fast carries risks. Standing still carries a larger one.', and a tidy closing moral. Paragraphs 5 and 7 switch to stiff, paraphraser-like prose ('There are three deliberate decisions that need to be made regarding which of these two competing scenarios will occur').

criteria.name: stories
criteria.reason: Analytic prompt, so a case study can serve as the story. Horace Mann's Prussian model and Cuban's Silicon Valley schools are both on topic, but each is a summary of a few sentences, and no single case carries the argument.

criteria.name: ideas_mechanism
criteria.reason: Names the existing fixes (retraining, wage insurance, UBI) and says why they fail ('treat the symptoms... rather than its cause'), then proposes public infrastructure, a shared core, and reversing the deployment order. It never says who pays, through what program, or why districts would adopt it.

criteria.name: structure_ending
criteria.reason: The close returns to the Spotify/Amazon/medicine opening ('Music, medicine, retail, news, and travel'), but the last line is a generic moral: 'The choice is ours, and it must be made deliberately and soon.' The three decisions are labeled inconsistently ('three key public decisions', then 'The third alternative').

fixes: Voice (up to +12): rewrite the antithesis sentences as plain claims. Examples: 'personalized learning is an investment in public infrastructure rather than a product' becomes 'Treat adaptive tutoring like the public library: publicly funded and free at the door'. Cut 'The shared core remains; the path to it varies.' and 'Moving too fast carries risks. Standing still carries a larger one.' Replace both em dashes in the modality sentence with commas or parentheses. Fix the broken 'will not only be left to the private market; rather' sentence and the 'which of these two competing scenarios' sentence in paragraph 5. Replace 'The choice is ours, and it must be made deliberately and soon.' with a last line that names the opening image again (one playlist per listener, one lesson per thirty students).

Ideas (up to +6): in the infrastructure and deployment-order paragraphs, name the delivery vehicle and payer for decision one, and say what makes a district adopt the tool rather than ignore it like earlier ed-tech (the Cuban problem you raise). If Enes has a real view or source on the funding channel (Title I, E-Rate, state contracts), ask him for it and use it. Do not invent a program or figure.

Case study and facts (up to +6, plus fact-gate risk): pick one case and tell it fully instead of three summaries. The Kestin et al. Harvard trial is the strongest: what the students did, what was measured, what 'twice as much' means. Use it to carry the 'binding constraint has loosened' paragraph. Check the PLOS ONE '28%' figure against Pierce and Cleary before submitting. Then either replace it with a statistic that actually shows a gap widened by ed-tech, or reword the 'mostly increased the gap' sentence so it only claims what the source shows.
